blocks.text: Understanding what actually happens between typing a prompt and receiving a response is not just academic curiosity, it directly explains why phrasing, word order, and structure genuinely change model output, the mechanical basis for everything the rest of this course teaches.

This topic walks through the pipeline a prompt passes through, tokenization, embedding, attention, transformer layers, and next token prediction, without requiring deep math, enough to build accurate intuition for why prompt engineering techniques actually work.
1. A Prompt Starts as Plain Text

blocks.alt: Raw prompt text passes through a tokenizer, producing a token sequence

blocks.text: Before a model can process anything, your raw prompt text gets broken into tokens, small chunks of text, by a tokenizer, this step is covered in full depth in the next topic, Tokens and Tokenization, for now the key point is that the model never actually sees your words directly, only this tokenized representation.
2. Tokens Become Vectors Through Embedding

blocks.alt: The token sequence goes through an embedding lookup, producing a sequence of vectors

blocks.text: Each token gets converted into a vector, a long list of numbers, through an embedding lookup, this vector representation is what lets the model perform mathematical operations on what started as plain text, tokens with related meanings tend to have vectors that are mathematically closer together.
3. Attention Weighs Relationships Between Tokens

blocks.alt: The token bank weighs its relationship to nearby tokens like river or money through attention

blocks.text: The attention mechanism lets the model weigh how much each token should influence its understanding of every other token, the word bank means something different next to river than it does next to money, attention is the mechanism that lets context like this actually shift how a token gets interpreted.
4. Passing Through Many Transformer Layers

blocks.alt: Input vectors pass through transformer layer 1, then layer 2, then many more layers

blocks.text: The vectors, now carrying attention informed context, pass through many stacked transformer layers, each layer refines the representation further, building progressively richer understanding of the prompt, a large model might have dozens of these layers stacked on top of each other.

blocks.text: 5. Predicting the Next Token

blocks.alt: The final hidden state produces a probability distribution over every possible next token

blocks.text: After passing through every layer, the model produces a probability distribution across its entire vocabulary, essentially a ranked guess at what token should come next, the model does not directly know facts or reason in the way a person does, it is fundamentally predicting the most probable continuation given everything that came before.
6. Generation Happens One Token at a Time

blocks.alt: One token is generated, appended to the sequence, and fed back into the model, repeating

blocks.text: A full response is not generated all at once, the model generates one token, appends it to the sequence, and feeds the entire updated sequence back through itself to generate the next token, this autoregressive loop repeats until a stopping condition is reached.

code.content:
# Simplified view of autoregressive generation
tokens = tokenize(prompt)
for step in range(max_new_tokens):
    next_token = model.predict_next(tokens)
    tokens.append(next_token)
    if next_token == END_OF_SEQUENCE:
        break

blocks.text: 7. Why Phrasing and Word Order Genuinely Matter

blocks.alt: A reordered or reworded prompt produces a different attention pattern and a different output

blocks.text: Because attention weighs relationships between tokens based on their actual positions and surrounding context, reordering a prompt, or rewording it even slightly, changes the attention pattern the model computes, which changes the probability distribution over next tokens at every single generation step, this is the mechanical reason prompt wording actually matters.

blocks.title: This is why prompt engineering is not superstition
blocks.content: Every technique covered later in this course, few-shot examples, clear structure, explicit constraints, works because it measurably shifts the attention patterns and resulting probability distributions this pipeline computes, not because of some vague notion of the model understanding intent.

blocks.text: 8. What This Means Practically for Prompt Engineering

Since the model builds its response token by token based on everything that came before, information placed earlier in a prompt genuinely shapes how later parts get interpreted, and the exact words chosen influence which tokens the model considers likely, this is the mechanical basis for placement and specificity mattering in prompt design.
9. The Full Pipeline, Summarized

Tokenize the raw text, convert tokens to vectors through embedding, refine those vectors through attention and many transformer layers, predict a probability distribution over the next token, generate one token, and repeat the entire process, this loop, running many times per response, is what happens behind every single model reply.
Worked Example

A developer notices that asking a model "Explain quantum computing. Keep it brief." sometimes produces a long, unfocused answer, while asking "In 2 sentences, explain quantum computing" reliably produces a short, focused answer.

Understanding the generation pipeline explains why, placing the length constraint first shapes the attention pattern from the very first generated token onward, the model is predicting each token conditioned on everything before it, so an early constraint has influence over the entire generation from the start, while a constraint added as an afterthought at the end has already lost that early shaping influence.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a model reasons or retrieves facts the way a person does, rather than predicting the most probable next token repeatedly
Placing an important constraint at the very end of a long prompt where it has less influence over early generated tokens
Ignoring that identical information reworded differently can produce meaningfully different outputs due to changed attention patterns
Treating the entire generation pipeline as an unexplainable black box rather than a predictable mechanism prompt engineering can work with

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt you have used before, rewrite it by moving the most important instruction to the very beginning instead of the end, run both versions against the same model, and compare whether the outputs differ.
Key Takeaway

A language model processes a prompt through tokenization, embedding, attention, and stacked transformer layers to predict one token at a time, this mechanical pipeline is exactly why wording, structure, and placement measurably change model output, giving prompt engineering a concrete, non mysterious foundation.
